modernizationNote: This pack matters on BOTH sides of a migration.
Run it on the LEGACY source to establish what weaknesses the system already had, and on the
GENERATED target to check whether they were carried across. A migration that faithfully
reproduces a SQL injection is a faithful migration and an insecure application.
Findings originating in legacy source should carry origin: 'legacy-inherited' so the report can
distinguish pre-existing debt from defects introduced by the modernization itself.

rules.title: Dynamic SQL executed from a constructed string
rules.why: Dynamic SQL assembled from parameters inside a stored procedure is injectable, and it runs with the procedure's privileges.
rules.falsePositiveHints: sp_executesql with declared @params is parameterized and safe. EXECUTE IMMEDIATE with USING bind variables is safe. The finding is concatenation into the statement text.

rules.title: Broad privilege grant
rules.pattern: (?i)GRANT\s+(ALL|DBA|SYSDBA|CONTROL|ALTER ANY|EXECUTE ANY|SELECT ANY)|TO\s+PUBLIC|WITH GRANT OPTION|EXECUTE AS\s+(OWNER|'dbo')
rules.why: GRANT ALL and TO PUBLIC discard least privilege; a single application-level flaw then reaches the whole database.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Setup scripts for a local development database are lower severity. Confirm whether the script is applied to production.

rules.title: Credential embedded in a SQL or DDL script
rules.why: Database account passwords in versioned scripts are readable by everyone with repository access and by CI logs.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Templated placeholders are fine. A literal password is a finding and requires rotation.

rules.title: Sensitive column stored without protection
rules.why: Sensitive identifiers and secrets in plaintext columns are exposed by any read access, any backup, and any dump.
rules.falsePositiveHints: A password column holding a bcrypt/argon2 digest is correct - check the length and how the application writes it. PII columns may be covered by transparent database encryption; verify rather than assume.

rules.title: Legacy dynamic SQL built by string construction
rules.why: 4GL/COBOL programs frequently build SQL text into a working variable and PREPARE it. If any part comes from a screen field, it is injectable - and the modernized code usually inherits the pattern.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Statements assembled purely from literals and program constants are safe. Trace whether an input field (screen, ARG_VAL, ACCEPT) reaches the string.

rules.title: Credential or connection detail in legacy source
rules.why: Legacy programs commonly hold database and user credentials inline. These are carried into modernized configuration unless deliberately extracted to a secret store.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Database name without credentials is Info. Confirm an actual secret value is present.

rules.title: Home-grown authentication or password comparison in legacy code
rules.why: Legacy authentication typically compares plaintext passwords with no hashing, salting, lockout or timing safety. Migrating this logic verbatim reproduces every weakness in the new stack.
rules.falsePositiveHints: This is the single most important legacy pattern to catch during a modernization. Do not port it - the remediation is to replace it with the target platform's identity provider, not to translate it.

rules.title: Filesystem or OS call from legacy code
rules.why: RUN/SYSTEM/Shell with a constructed argument is command injection; file paths built from input are traversal.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Fixed literal paths and commands are Info. The finding is a variable reaching the argument.

rules.title: Screen or terminal input consumed without validation
rules.why: Legacy screen input relied on the terminal form for constraints. Once the logic is exposed over HTTP by a modernization, that implicit boundary is gone and the constraint must become explicit server-side validation.
rules.falsePositiveHints: Not a vulnerability in the legacy system itself. It IS a required action item for the modernized target - report it as a migration-risk item, and record the field lengths and types so the target validation can mirror the real schema.

rules.title: Home-grown or trivially reversible encryption
rules.why: Hand-rolled obfuscation offers no confidentiality. Data protected this way should be treated as plaintext.
rules.falsePositiveHints: XOR used for a checksum or bit manipulation is not encryption. Read the routine's purpose.
